div.p: Multi-core processors deliver higher performance with a smaller footprint and lower power consumption making them attractive for modern real-time embedded applications. In real-time computing achieving higher performance alongside sustaining system correctness, predictability and meeting all hard deadlines are very crucial. Concurrent access of the tasks to shared-resources (e.g., memory structure, DMA, peripherals) by multiple tasks running on different cores induces higher blocking time, which increases the worst-case execution (WCET) time of tasks and can cause missing hard deadlines, consequently resulting in system failure. The tasks blocking time, perpetuated cache evictions and communication with slow I/O peripherals increase the worst-case execution time of real-time tasks. Ultimately these added overheads in WCET reduce task-set schedulability. In this paper, we propose an Inter-task Affinity-aware Task Allocation (IATA) algorithm, which groups the tasks considering their constraints, dependencies, and preferences; and allocate these groups on multiple cores such that the additive overheads in WCET are minimized. The tasks handling slow I/O peripherals are assigned to a dedicated I/O core and to reduce cache evictions the tasks with higher priority, and sharing data-sets are allocated on scratch-pad RAM. In the evaluation of our algorithm, we compare our proposed algorithm IATA with blocking-agnostic Best Fit Decreasing (BFD) task allocation algorithm. The results reveal that our proposed (IATA) algorithm allocates on the average 97.5% more task-sets than BFD, increases schedulability and reduces processor utilization.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Due to the limitation of silicon and higher power dissipation; a further increase in the operating frequency of unicore processors is not favorable. To meet industry's higher performance requirements, embedded system designers are moving their existing designs to multi-core platforms. The real-time applications developed for uni-core processors with decades of efforts cannot be used directly on multi-core platforms. Multi-core platforms have a number of on-chip sharedresources (buses, cache, memory, peripheral, etc.) used by multiple on-chip cores. Concurrent mutually exclusive access to these shared-resources may block real-time tasks running on the same or other on-chip cores. Such blocking of the tasks can produce a deadlock, prolong worst-case execution time (WCET) and can cause missing a deadline. Prolonged execution time and perpetuated blocking due to concurrent access of shared-resource increases processor utilization and ultimately reduce the schedulability of the real-time task. The three most used real-time scheduling schemes in multi-core processors are Global Scheduling, Partitioned Scheduling, and Semi-Partitioned Scheduling. In global partitioned scheduling a single scheduler and tasks ready-queue is used to schedule task jobs on all available cores and task migration to other cores is allowed. In semi-partitioned scheduling a limited number of tasks are allowed to migrate between cores, while keeping other tasks static on multiple cores. In the partitioned scheduling, tasks are allocated statically on multiple cores, each core runs standalone scheduler, task read-queue, and task migration is not allowed. Partitioned Earlier Deadline First (P-EDF), Partitioned Rate Monotonic (P-RMS) and Partitioned Deadline Monotonic (P-DM) scheduling schemes are extended versions of uni-core scheduling schemes proposed in [1], [2] and can be used with minimal changes while porting a unicore real-time application to multi-core platforms. Partitioned scheduling is equally efficient for new multi-core designs. In partitioned scheduling, each on-chip core can use distinct Real-Time Operating system (RTOS), and scheduling schemes which make it more attractive for hard real-time applications [3]. A number of task allocation algorithms are proposed [4] but most of them assume independent tasks and ignore blocking caused by shared-resources access, precedence dependencies, etc.

The blocking time can be bounded using multi-core synchronization protocols such as Multiprocessor Priority Ceiling Protocols (MPCP) [5] and Multiprocessor Stack Resource Policy (MSRP) [6]. The upper-bound of blocking time can be reduced significantly by allocating mutually dependent realtime tasks on similar cores.

Modern multi-core platforms provide on-chip Scratch-Pad Memory (SPM) along with the multilevel caches. Cache memories assist processor in bringing execution code and data near to the processor. On the other hand, unpredictable cache evictions are the significant sources of nondeterministic execution of a real-time task and cause an increase in worstcase execution time.

In this paper, we are proposing an efficient framework for statically allocating real-time tasks on multi-core processor such that blocking of the tasks reduces significantly. To nullify overheads in WCET due to the cache evictions, we propose to allocate timing sensitive tasks and tasks with higher repetition rate (higher priority tasks in Partitioned Rate Monotonic Scheduling) onto SPM.

A motivational example is shown in Figure 1 and 2. In Figure 1 a typical case is shown where real-time tasks are allocated on a multi-core processor using Inter-task affinityagnostic technique. The tasks sharing a resource R1 are allocated on all available cores. When a task T1 locks the resource R1 all other tasks T4, T7, and T9 get blocked when trying to access this already locked shared-resource R1. Suppose the task T7 is get blocked and put in wait-state then this task will block all the other task indirectly on this core, e.g., T6, T8. Such kind of blocking is called indirect blocking. Moreover task T1, T4, T2, T5, T7, T9 are using Inter-Processor Communication (IPC) which is also overhead to WCET of these tasks. On the other hand in figure 2 a best case task allocation is shown, where the tasks sharing a resource and having IPC dependency are put on the same processor. Practically this approach reduces blocking time of a task and increase schedulability. To reduce the indirect blocking of the tasks due to longer duration tasks handling I/O peripherals, we propose to allocate all I/O task on a dedicated I/O core.
Our contributions in this paper include,

• We propose an efficient task allocation framework which reduces task blocking time and increase task schedulability. • Our framework reduces IPC and cache evictions overheads. • Our proposed framework can be used with P-RMS, P-EDF, MPCP, and MSRP.

• We provide a comprehensive results comparison with inter-task affinity-agnostic task allocation technique BFD [7]. The paper is organized as follows. In section II an overview of related work is presented, in section III task synchronization and calculation of blocking time is explained, section IV describes the system model with basic definitions. Section V provides details regarding task allocation strategies while section VI provides insight into the experimental evaluation and results. Finally, the paper is concluded in section VII.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: In this section, we provide a brief overview of the relevant work done in the area of task scheduling, task allocation, synchronization of shared-resources, and scheduling schemes used in multi-core real-time devices. Uni-core scheduling schemes namely Rate-Monotonic (RM) and Earlier Deadline First (EDF) were introduced by Liu and Layland [1] and can be used in partitioned scheduling with the support of multicore synchronization protocols(section III). In Partitioned-RM scheduling a set of n periodic tasks is schedulable if

, hence under RM the scheduling utilization bound of a core approaches to 0.69 for larger number of tasks. The experiments performed by Lehoczky et al. [8] revealed that the Liu and Layland bound is tight and the utilization bound can increase up to 0.88 in some scenarios. Leung and Whitehead proposed Deadline Monotonic [2] scheduling which is an extension of RM with the flexibility of relative deadlines less than tasks' periods. The schedulability test under DM is determined using C i /D i ≤ n(2 1/n -1). In Partitioned-EDF, each job of a real-time task is prioritized in the ready queue according to the relative deadline. Partitioned-EDF is multi-core version of uniprocessor EDF [1] . EDF introduces an overhead at run-time due to dynamic priority assignment but still provides higher processor schedulability than the Partitioned-RM scheme. For the sufficient and necessary schedulability tests, task response time formula was introduced in [9], [10] .
div.formula: R i = e i + i-1 j=1 R i T j × e j ≤ d i ∀1 ≤ i ≤ n(1)
div.p: Where R i is the response time, e i is the worst-case execution time, and T i , D i are the period and deadline of a task respectively.
Demand bound function (dbf) proposed by Baruah et al. [11]. is used for necessary and sufficient scheduling test in Partitioned-EDF.
div.formula: dbf (L) = n i=1 L -d i T i + 1 × e i ≤ L ∀L > 0 (2)
div.p: L is a time within the interval [t, t + L] and dbf is the processor-time required in the interval [t, t + L] that needs to be executed with d i ≤ (t + L).

A number of task allocation schemes have been presented in the literature. Huang et al [12] proposed a heuristic to improve the speed-up factor of multi-core processors considering shared-resources oriented task allocation. Lakshmanan et al [13], [14] proposed a task synchronization aware partitioned heuristic for fixed priority scheduling by extending Multiprocessor Priority Ceiling Protocols (MPCP) [5]. A method similar to ours is presented by Nemati et al [15] in which tasks are arranged in groups using the heuristic cost function, and these groups of tasks are entirely allocated on one processor. Hsiu et al [16] proposed a semi-partitioned scheduling scheme by separating tasks accessing shared-resources from independent tasks and an RPC like priority based resource sharing mechanism made sure that higher priority tasks are blocked only single time by a lower priority task. Our proposed work uses partitioned scheduling while the work presented in [16] uses semi-partitioned scheduling. In [17] an optimized model of task allocation is presented for the soft real-time system, while our proposed work focuses on hard real-time systems. Saifullah et al. [18] proposed task splitting method for scheduling both partitioned-RMS and partitioned-EDF scheduling schemes. Another shared-resources aware task allocation scheme for partitioned scheduling was introduced in [19] by Buttazzo et al.

div.head: III. TASK SYNCHRONIZATION IN MULTI-CORE PLATFORM
div.p: When a task tries to access a shared-resource, and the shared-resource is already locked by another task in the system, then this task is suspended or put on wait-state (spin), and the task is resumed when the shared-resource is released by the task previously locked it. When a task running on one core is blocked by another task running on the same core then this blocking is called local blocking and when this task is blocked by a task which is running on another core, then this blocking is called remote blocking. Multi-core synchronization protocols are used along with the partitioned scheduling schemes to bound the blocking time. The two wellknown multi-core synchronization protocols are MPCP [5] and MSRP [20]. Due to space limitations, we are skipping the details of these protocols but can be found in [5] and [20]. In the MPCP protocol which is extended from PCP [21], a blocked task is suspended, put in the global waiting queue and is resumed when the shared-resource is unlocked. The equation 3 provides the formula to calculate the blocking time B i experienced by the task τ i when it is blocked on a sharedresource. The more details of this equation can be found in the protocol definition [5].
div.formula: B i = n G i β l i + n G i β g i,k + nc G i,k T i T k βH glob i,k +nh G i,r,k T i T k β glob i,k + min n G i +1,n G k β glob i,k(3)
div.p: The Stack Resource Policy (SRP) [22] was proposed by Baker for uni-processor shared-resources synchronization, later extended as MSRP by Gai et al. [20] for multi-core processors. The MSRP protocols uses an additional constraint called preemption level λ i , where a task τ i can preempt a task τ j only if λ i > λ j . In the MSRP protocols, a blocked task is not suspended as in MPCP but is put into waiting state called spinning state. The upper bound of blocking time B i , calculated using multi-core synchronization protocols adds up in WCET. The schedulability tests [1] designed for P-RMS and P-EDF with independent task-sets are modified by adding blocking time factors B i , and are given in equation 4 and 5 respectively.

div.head: IV. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: In this section we define the task model used in this paper, multi-core platform information, and basic definitions used in allocation framework.

div.head: A. Task Model
div.p: We are using a sporadic task-set ψ having real-time tasks characterized by computation time {e 1 , e 2 ......e n }, periods of {T 1 , T 2 , . . . . . . , T n }, relative deadline {d 1 , d 2 , . . . . . . , d n }, and priority {ρ 1 , ρ 2 . . . . . . , ρ n } i.e. τ i = (e i , d i , T i , ρ i ). This task-set is allocated on a multi-core processor P having P = {P 1 , P 2 ...P m } , m identical cores running at the same speed. These cores are interconnected using system buses and shared memory. The considered multi-core processor has onchip multi-level cache and scratchpad-RAM.

div.head: B. Definitions
div.p: • Inter-Task Shared-Resources Affinity (A r ): Multiple tasks can share a single on-chip or peripheral resource. The mutually exclusive access to these resources is granted through semaphores. Let two tasks τ i , τ j are sharing a single shared-resource R k which is guarded by a semaphore S k , having the duration D i,h,k , D j,h,k of Z i,h,k , Z j,h,k are the h th critical sections of tasks τ i &τ j , accessing the shared-resource R k then A r i,j is the intertask shared-resources affinity between task τ i and τ j sharing resource R k . The µ r is the normalizing factor which is calculated as
div.formula: µ r = [max(D i,j,h,k ) -min(D i,j,h,k )] -1 A r i,j = µ r n h=1 D i,h,k + n h=1 D j,h,k(7)
div.p: The value of A r i,j = 0 for all the tasks not sharing any resource with any other task.

• Inter-Task Precedence Affinity (A p ): The execution of tasks having precedence dependencies (parent-child relation) on multiple distinct cores of a multi-core processor required inter-core messaging for synchronization. These inter-core messages induce unnecessary delays which increase worst-case execution time and increase processor utilization. Allocating all such tasks having precedence dependencies to the same core decreases inter-core messaging overheads. Suppose two tasks τ i , τ j having precedence dependency then
div.formula: A p i,j = 1, if τ i , τ j have prec. dependency. 0, otherwise. (8
div.p: • Inter-Task Shared-Data Affinity(A d ): In many real-time applications (e.g., Digital Signal Processing, Image Processing, Tabular Data) some tasks process large size of data-sets. When multiple tasks are processing these datasets on the same core, it can reduce cache eviction (by reusing same data-sets) [23] and even processing time can be reduced by allocating these data-sets on local scratchpad RAM. If two tasks τ i , τ j are accessing a data-set DS r of size SZ r bytes then
div.formula: A d i,j = µ d n r=1 SZ r,i,j(9)
div.p: µ d is the normalizing factor which is calculated as µ d = [max(SZ r,i,j ) -min(SZ r,i,j )]
• Inter-Task Total Affinity Factor(ITTAF): The weighted sum of all three factors computed in equation 7, 8 and 9 is called Inter-Task Total Affinity Factor (ITTAF) and is represented by ω i,j
div.formula: ω i,j = λ r A r i,j + λ p A p i,j + λ d A d i,j(10)
div.p: where λ r , λ p , λ d are the weights of each factor. The value of ω i,j is used to make task groups called macrotasks. • Inter-Task Total Affinity Matrix(ITAM): The ITTAF of all the tasks to be allocated is calculated and is arranged in a matrix form and is called Inter-Task Total Affinity Matrix(ITAM), The ITAM is used during the task grouping process. IT AM (i, j) = {ω i,j , | ω i,j = ω j,i ∀τ i , τ j ∈ ψ} • Dependent task-set ψ d : The set of all the tasks having an inter-task affinity with any other tasks in the system e.g. ψ d ⊆ ψ ∀ ω i,j > 0 . • Independent task-set ψ i : The set of all the tasks having ω i,j = 0 with all other task in the system e.g. ψ i ⊆ ψ ∀ ω i,j = 0 . • Peripheral I/O task-set ψ io : All the tasks accessing onchip or external peripheral. • Macrotasks: Suppose the task τ 1 has strong affinity with τ 2 (ω 1,2 > 0), and task τ 2 has strong affinity with τ 3 (ω 2,3 > 0) but the task τ 3 have no affinity with the task τ 1 (ω 3,1 = 0). The Algorithm 1 depending upon the ITTAF, combines all such dependent tasks in groups of tasks called Macrotasks.

div.head: V. PROPOSED ALGORITHM FOR TASK ALLOCATION
div.p: In this section, we explain our proposed Inter-task Affinitycentric Task Allocation (IATA) algorithm for the task allocation on an AMP homogeneous uniform multi-core platform. The algorithm IATA can be used under partitioned-RMS and partitioned-EDF scheduling schemes along with the MPCP and MSRP. The algorithm uses uni-core synchronization protocol PCP and MSR when the dependent tasks are allocated on the same core of the processor. The value of remote blocking time valid for globally shared-resources is different for both protocols as explained in section III. Therefore, the algorithm uses global blocking time formula whenever tasks are blocked on globally shared-resource. The more details of the calculation of blocking time under MSRP synchronization protocols is given in [22].

div.head: A. Initial Setup
div.p: In the initial setup of algorithm, The ITAM is constructed by calculating ω i,j for all tasks in the task-set ψ using equation 10. The appropriate weight values of λ r , λ p , λ d can be used, e.g. setting λ r = λ p = λ d = 1 makes all three affinity weights equally effective in ITTAF calculation. All the tasks τ i having IT T AF > 0 with other tasks in the system are grouped to make macrotasks. By examining the mutual ITTAF values of all the task in ITAM; the pairs of tasks are made such that ϕ k = [τ i , τ j ] = max(IT AM (i, j)) where ϕ k ⊂ Ψ, and all the task-pairs are sorted in decreasing affinity order Φ = {ϕ 1 , ..., ϕ k , ..., ϕ n }. All the task ψ io handling I/O peripherals are allocated on the m'th core of multi-core processor which is dedicated as an I/O core.

div.head: C. Algorithm 2
div.p: In this step, the algorithm allocates macrotasks on multiple available cores. On line 2, the algorithm performs the schedulability tests. For the schedulability test, all the tasks in macrotask to be allocated and all the tasks already allocated to the current core are grouped to make a task-set. Then the schedulability test described in equation 4, 5 and 6 depending upon the scheduling scheme in use are performed. The value of B i is calculated using equations given in MPCP and MSRP Algorithm 2: Allocate macrotasks on available processor cores Input : protocols. Once the schedulability test is passed the algorithm selects next macrotask and tries to allocate it on the same core. If the macrotask is unable to allocate entirely on current core, then algorithm adds new core to the system and allocate this macrotask. In case, the macrotask is unable to allocate entirely on one core (due to exhausted utilization capacity or macrotask is too big to fit on an empty core), then the macrotask is split using the SplitMacroTask function. The core with maximum available capacity is selected, and this function is called repeatedly until the macrotask become small enough to fit on the available core.

div.head: D. Finalization
div.p: After the task assignments completed on all available cores. The tasks prone to extensive cache evictions, identified from the design specifications are allocated on scratch-pad RAM. Using the compiler and linker directives the code and data of all these tasks are placed onto on-chip scratch-pad memory (SPM) depending upon the available SPM size. All the independent task ψ i are allocated on available cores using the Best Fit bin-packing method.

div.head: VI. EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
div.p: The experimental evaluation of the task allocation strategy is performed on a multi-core embedded platform from the Taxes Instruments TMDXEVM6678LE which has an eightcore DSP processor TMS320C6678 running at 1.0 GHz. The SysBios ver.6.35.01.29 developed by Taxes Instruments is used as the real-time kernel for the evaluation of the proposed IATA algorithm. The selected multi-core processor has a multi-level cache, on-chip scratch-pad memory (SPM), shared memory and externally connected DDR. The L2 cache is disabled and is used as scratch-pad memory. We have used task-sets generated using industry standard real benchmark MiBench [24] with multiple timing parameters according to the method proposed in [25]. To evaluate the average performance of proposed algorithm, we create, symmetrical uniform distribution of utilization using UUniFast algorithm proposed in [26]. The utilization cap of task-sets is selected from 0.1 to 0.9 with an increment of 0.1. The worstcase execution time e i for each task is calculated using the relation e i = u i × T i . For fixed priority scheduling, priorities are calculated using Rate Monotonic scheduling scheme [1]. The task periods are generated similar to the method used by [22]. After assigning timing constraints to the tasks, shared-resources constraints are added. A percentage (50% to 80%) of the tasks is selected for sharing 1 to 4 resources. critical sections of the length selected randomly between (10 to 30) percent of WCET are added. The precedence order of the tasks is generated randomly between 30% to 50% of the total tasks in a task-set, and 10 percent of total tasks are declared as cache sensitive. A number of tasks are selected to allocate on scratch-pad RAM. The proposed task allocation algorithm IATA is evaluated under partitioned-RMS and partitioned-EDF scheduling schemes along with MSRP and MPCP multicore shared-resources synchronization protocols. The results show that the blocking time caused by global shared-resources is reduced significantly by allocating task using IATA as compared to Best Fitting Decreasing (BFD) [7] task allocation technique. The BFD is inter-task affinity-agnostic technique. Therefore, the possibility of allocating inter-dependent tasks on multiple cores is higher than inter-task affinity-centric IATA. With the increasing number of cores and tasks sharing the same resource, the span of tasks allocated on multiple different cores also increases, which eventually results in more global shared-resources. It can also be inferred from the MPCP and MSRP protocols definition that blocking time of a real-time task is increased by increasing number of globally shared-resources. The results in Figure 4 show that IATA with varying scheduling schemes, synchronization protocols, number of cores and number of shared-resources can allocate on the average 97.5% more tasks than the BFD. These results show that the task-set which could not be scheduled using BFD can still be scheduled using IATA. The algorithm is evaluated using 2, 4, 6 and 8 active cores, while the shared-resources are varied from 4 to 40. The number of tasks having precedence dependencies is kept constant at 50% of total number of tasks. The evaluation results revealed that IATA provides higher task schedulable ratio than the BFD. The results in Figure 5 show that IATA under P-RMS and P-EDF can allocate more tasks than BFD. Therefore, the task-set which is not schedulable using BFD task allocation is still able to schedule using our proposed strategy. The test results shown in Figure 5 The proposed algorithm groups all tasks which have higher ITTAF and allocate them on the same core which reduces, 1) task's remote blocking time due to shared resources, 2) intercore communication, and 3) caches misses. These time saving factors add up to reduce total processor busy time, which is consumed to schedule additional tasks. The shared-resources aware task allocation by IATA reduces the ratio of globally shared-resource to the total shared-resources in the system as shown in Figure 6. The experimental results show that task allocated by IATA results in 100% less global shared-resources on the average. Scratch-pad memories(SPM) provides a way to quickly access required data and code, near to the processor, while increased cache evictions result in higher cache miss rate and cache controller have to fetch required code and data from main memory frequently which prolong the task execution and increases worst-case execution time. The results are shown in Figure 7 shows that tasks executed from SPM utilize less processor time than the tasks executed from the cache memory. When the tasks communicating with each other are allocated on different cores, they use inter-core communication channels to exchange information. Such tasks utilizing inter-core communication, are allocated on the same core, which reduces time required to acquire IPC channel and transfer data. In this way, the overall execution time of the tasks is reduced, and schedulability is increased. The timing comparison of inter-task communication is shown in Figure 8 for both IATA and BFD strategies. Different task sets with varying precedence constraints of 10% to 70% are tested on 4 and 8 active cores. The results shows that task sets allocated using IATA, consume significantly less time as compared to task sets allocated using BFD.

The proposed algorithm is evaluated using different weight values of λ r , λ p , λ d but due to space limitations, the results produced using λ r = λ p = λ d = 1 weight values are presented in this paper. The weight values can be changed from 0 to 1 depending upon the task set and requirements.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: Achieving higher performance along with meeting the hard deadlines of real-time tasks is very vital in hard real-time systems. The CPU time wasted in waiting to access global shared resources, inter-core communication and cache misses increases processor utilization, which eventually decreases number of schedulable tasks on available cores. The Intertask Affinity-centric Task Allocation (IATA) algorithm considers inter-task dependencies and preferences (shared-resources, Inter-core communication, cache evictions) to reduces processor wasted time and utilization significantly. It makes possible to reduce worst-case execution time, and on the average 97.5% more tasks can be allocated using IATA as compared to conventional task allocation strategy BFD. The results of experiments have reflected that proposed strategy reduces global shared-resources, inter-core communication time and execution time of timing-critical tasks.

Use of the partitioned scheduling, make it simpler to use uni-processor scheduling schemes directly on multi-core platforms, saving plenty of time in re-tuning and re-testing the already developed embedded applications. In the future work, we will focus on run-time task allocation strategies for global and semi-partitioned scheduling schemes with different evolving synchronization protocols.
